Triggers.value: Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to erase the memory of the event
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have failed in my most important role in life
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette: The collapse had happened without warning during a routine team briefing. One moment Mai was pointing at quarterly deliverables; the next, her chest seized, her vision tunneled, and she slid to the floor. Emergency responders arrived within minutes, dragging her onto a gurney that felt impossibly cold against her back. Inside the resuscitation bay, the sharp, metallic scent of antiseptic and alcohol wipes overwhelmed her senses. Struggling to breathe, she felt the cold slide of a plastic collar around her neck, then the sharp pinch of a needle entering her arm for the emergency drip. For three days, she floated in and out of consciousness, anchored only by the hiss of oxygen lines and the relentless chill of the critical care unit. When she finally woke, the doctors pronounced her lucky to have survived the sudden respiratory failure, but Mai felt something fundamental snap. At first, the fear was manageable, but it quickly calcified into a rigid pattern of survival. Whenever a cold draft or the faint antiseptic of a colleague’s sanitizer crossed her desk, Mai’s immediate response was to rigidly monitor her thoughts for any slip toward madness, while simultaneously attempting to erase the moment from her mind and avoiding any physical examination. These environmental cues did not merely startle her; they forced the fragmented recall of the ICU to surface, pulling vivid flashes of the needle’s entry and the suffocating silence forward, entirely stripped of contextual image. Each time the cold triggered a spike of panic, Mai interpreted it as undeniable proof that her body had been permanently damaged, convincing her that her life was irrevocably destroyed. Because she became certain she had failed her most important roles as a project manager and a wife, the memory of the illness warped further; the story felt completely unreal, as if a broken body could not possibly hold a coherent past. The raw emotional surges that returned without any accompanying image reinforced this distortion, convincing her that her physical vulnerability was absolute and that her life was truly ruined. As the unanchored terror of those fragmented moments pooled in her chest, her baseline arousal spiked, making the faintest medical scent or temperature drop instantly register as a life-threatening trigger. Her relentless attempts to scrub the event from her awareness only fractured the timeline further, leaving her with terrifying blanks between moments of unbearable, hyper-detailed clarity. This constant surveillance and avoidance of medical settings convinced her that she had definitively failed her role, because the strategies designed to keep her safe were the very ones guaranteeing her professional isolation. By continuously policing her internal state and shutting down exposure, Mai amplified her physiological sensitivity, ensuring that the triggers themselves grew more potent and harder to withstand. Over eight months, the loop tightened around her daily life. Coordinating a hospital wing renovation for a client project, she began declining every required site inspection at the medical center, citing scheduling conflicts. This avoidance fractured her standing with the client and forced her husband to repeatedly cover her absences, transforming her internal dread into concrete occupational and relational erosion. Mai no longer trusted her own mind, convinced that confronting the trauma would finally shatter what remained of her health. What finally drove her to therapy was a moment of sheer paralysis at a company retreat, where a cooler of saline solutions sat beside the coffee urn. Terrified that another collapse was imminent and desperate to reclaim her career and her marriage, Mai sat in the intake room with her hands folded tightly in her lap, hoping someone could help her untangle the thread before her life unraveled completely.
